title: Food counted late: what happens?
hook: A population reacts to food counted 4 years ago. Does it still settle at its limit?

knows: logistic growth is an S-curve that levels off at a limit
doesNotKnow: that delayed feedback can make a stable system boom and bust

misconception: Logistic growth always settles smoothly at its limit.
objective: The learner can explain that when growth responds to old information the population overshoots and swings, and that swings start once growth rate times delay passes about 1.6 (pi/2).
keyState: Delay set to 4 years with growth 0.5 (swings between 2.90 and 0.07 times the limit), then growth lowered to 0.2 with the same delay (settles at the limit).

claims.text: Toy model: a population N, shown as a multiple of its food limit, grows at rate r N (1 - N delayed) where the delayed term is the population from the delay ago (the delayed logistic of Hutchinson). It starts at half the limit.
claims.source: Hutchinson (1948) delay logistic; stated on the stage before the prediction ('Toy: population as a share of its food limit, food counted late.'). Start 0.5 and constant history 0.5 are choices in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: With growth 0.5 a year and a 4-year delay, the population keeps swinging, reaching about 2.9 times the limit and falling to about 0.07 times the limit.
claims.source: Euler integration dt = 0.01 yr, 60 years, window years 30-60 (node, same sim() as Demo.tsx): max 2.895, min 0.0722. Deterministic; no random seed. Brief figures 2.9 and 0.07 match.

claims.text: With growth 0.2 a year and the same 4-year delay, the population settles at the limit.
claims.source: Same sim(): window years 30-60 max 1.0095, min 0.9973 (node).

claims.text: The swings start once growth rate times delay passes about 1.6 (pi/2 = 1.571): 0.5 x 4 = 2 swings; 0.2 x 4 = 0.8 settles.
claims.source: Linear stability of the delayed logistic, oscillations sustained when r x tau > pi/2 (Murray, Mathematical Biology I). Checked numerically: r 0.5 with tau 3 (1.5) still decays, tau 3.2 (1.6) is still near the threshold.

claims.text: The population reacts to old food, so it overshoots before the signal arrives. Real boom-and-bust cycles in animals such as lemmings have other causes too.
claims.source: Mechanism of the delay equation; the caveat is from the brief (reindeer and lemming cycles have other causes). The lesson names only the delay model.

recall.question: Why can a population swing far above and below its limit if it responds to food counted years ago?
options: It reacts to old information, so it keeps growing after food has run short
Its growth rate keeps changing at random
The limit itself moves up and down
recall.why: The correction arrives late, so the population overshoots, then overcorrects. Slower growth or a shorter delay lets it settle.
